newsitem.title: UK: Europe's chemical investment seen flat in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Europe's chemical investment seen flat in 1997.

text.p: Capital investment by Europe's chemical industry is expected to be little changed in 1997 from 1996 levels, Britain's Chemical Industries Association (CIA) said on Wednesday.

CIA economist Nick Sturgeon told the association's annual investment intentions conference that "while the chemicals outlook in the UK and Europe is fairly buoyant for 1997, investment is growing but not strongly."
The CIA expects production of chemicals in western Europe to rise by 3.3 percent in 1997 after a sluggish one percent rise in 1996. Output in Britain is expected to climb by three percent.

He said there was "some downside to the positive picture painted for the outlook in western Europe reflecting policy uncertainties as countries struggle to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria for EMU."
"It is very likely that such uncertainties are being reflected in the current investment forecasts for the industry."
Sturgeon said investment by the European industry in the 1990s had been relatively weak, amid industry restructuring and little pressure on production capacity.

The CIA said investment by Britain's chemical industry actually fell in 1996 from 1995, dropping by 0.6 percent in real terms. This compares with an increase in capital spending of 14 percent predicted by companies at the start of 1996.
Based on figures supplied by other national federations, Britain's capital investment performance last year was the weakest of any major chemicals producer.
Investment in France rose by around seven percent in real terms, in the Netherlands by around 13 percent, in Spain by 12 percent, in the U.S. by 11 percent and Japan by nearly 12 percent.
Investment in Germany rose by around one percent.
The CIA said investment in the UK this year is expected to increase by around five percent, again well behind most of its main competitors.

France is expected to increase investment this year by around six percent and the Netherlands, Spain and the U.S. by around 10 percent. German capital investment is forecast to rise by around one percent, while in Japan it is predicted to decline slightly in real terms.
